I am a control theorist currently serving as a Postdoctoral Research Fellow at Monash University (Clayton), working with A/Prof. Liz Ratnam.
I obtained a PhD in Engineering from the Australian National University for my work on negative imaginary systems theory and its applications, under the supervision of Prof. Ian Petersen and the co-supervision of Dr. Igor Vladimirov.
Prior to joining Monash University, I was a Postdoctoral Research Associate at the University of Sydney, where I worked with Prof. Ian Manchester.
My research interests include nonlinear systems, discrete-time systems, hybrid systems, learning-based control, multi-agent systems, and power systems.

title: Research Portfolio
text:
My research focuses on the control of negative imaginary (NI) systems, which naturally arise in many physical engineering systems.
I have established several theoretical results on the stability of NI systems under different control scenarios. More recently, I have been exploring how these ideas can be extended to modern control settings, where computation, learning, and digital implementation play a central role.
My work has demonstrated its utility across a range of engineering systems, including nanopositioning in atomic force microscopy, robotic control, and power systems.






Negative Imaginary Systems
Bridging the gap between robust continuous-time theory and practical digital implementation for flexible structures.

Key Themes

1. Negative Imaginary Systems
I investigate the properties of Negative Imaginary (NI) systems, which are crucial for the control of flexible structures and highly resonant systems. * Focus: Extending NI theory to discrete-time domains and zero-order hold sampling. * Application: Nanopositioning stages and flexible robotic arms.


2. Absolute Stability & Energy Shaping
I work on stability criteria for nonlinear systems, using potential energy shaping techniques to stabilize mechanical systems without canceling natural dynamics. * Focus: Absolute stability of nonlinear NI systems. * Goal: Robust controllers that preserve the physical intuition of the system.

title: Discrete-Time Negative Imaginary Systems
text:
The Challenge: Controlling Flexible Structures
Many high-precision engineering systems—such as atomic force microscopes (AFM), optical mirrors, and flexible robotic arms—are characterized by highly resonant dynamics. These systems are often modeled as collections of springs and masses.
Negative Imaginary (NI) systems theory provides a powerful tool for controlling these structures. The key benefit of NI controllers is robust stability: they guarantee stability even if the system has unmodeled high-frequency modes (spillover), provided the system remains NI.

title: Discrete-Time Negative Imaginary Systems
section: The Gap: The Digital Implementation Problem
text:
The Gap: The Digital Implementation Problem
While NI theory is well-established for continuous-time (analog) systems, modern control is almost exclusively implemented using digital computers.
Directly discretizing a continuous NI system (e.g., using Tustin’s method) often destroys the “Negative Imaginary” property. This leads to a dangerous gap: a controller proven stable in theory may become unstable when implemented digitally.

title: Discrete-Time Negative Imaginary Systems
text:
My Contribution: A Discrete-Time Framework
My research develops a rigorous framework for Discrete-Time Negative Imaginary Systems, specifically focusing on the effects of Zero-Order Hold (ZOH) sampling.
We have established conditions under which the NI property is preserved during sampling, allowing for the direct digital design of robust controllers.






NoteDefinition: Discrete-Time NI System



A square real rational proper transfer function matrix \(M(z)\) is Discrete-Time Negative Imaginary if:

\(M(z)\) has no poles in \(\{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| > 1\}\).
For all \(\theta \in (0, \pi)\) such that \(j(M(e^{j\theta}) - M^*(e^{j\theta}))\) is Hermitian, we have: \[
j(M(e^{j\theta}) - M^*(e^{j\theta})) \geq 0
\]

This condition ensures that the “phase lag” of the system behaves similarly to a passive system, but shifted by 90 degrees.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
section: 1. What is a Negative Imaginary System?
text:
1. What is a Negative Imaginary System?
Negative Imaginary (NI) systems are a broad class of dynamical systems defined by how they exchange energy with the environment.
A physical interpretation of the NI property is via the work-energy balance relation. A general nonlinear system (with input \(u\) and output \(y\)) is NI if there exists a storage function \(V(x) \geq 0\) such that:
\[
\dot{V}(x) \leq u^\top \dot{y}
\]

Left Side (\(\dot{V}\)): The rate of change of the system’s internal stored energy \(V\), including kinetic and potential energy.
Right Side (\(u^\top \dot{y}\)): The rate of change of the work done (the power injected) by the input force (\(u\)).

title: Negative Imaginary Systems
text:
Why is this useful?
The most powerful feature of NI theory is the Simple Stability Condition.
If you connect a Negative Imaginary Plant \(G(s)\) with a Negative Imaginary Controller \(C(s)\) in a positive feedback loop, the closed-loop system is stable if and only if the DC Gain condition is met:
\[
\lambda_{max}(G(0)C(0)) < 1
\]
Implication: This guarantees Robust Stability. Even if the structure has high-frequency resonance modes that you didn’t model (spillover), the system remains stable as long as those modes maintain the NI phase property.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems
text:
My Contribution: The Discrete-Time Frontier
While the continuous-time theory above is well-established, implementing these controllers on digital hardware presents a challenge.

The Problem
Directly discretizing an NI system (e.g., via Tustin transformation) often destroys the NI phase property. This means a digital controller might cause instability even if the continuous design was perfect.


My Solution: ZOH-NI Framework
My research developed the Discrete-Time Negative Imaginary (DT-NI) framework specifically for systems with Zero-Order Hold (ZOH) samplers.

Definition: We proposed a frequency-domain definition for DT-NI systems involving the unit circle.
Preservation: We proved conditions under which ZOH sampling preserves the NI property.
Synthesis: We developed methods to synthesize digital controllers that guarantee closed-loop stability for sampled-data NI systems.



Key Papers on this Topic

K. Shi, I. R. Petersen, and I. G. Vladimirov, “Discrete-time negative imaginary control systems using zero-order hold sampling,” Submitted to Automatica, 2025.
K. Shi, et al. “Discrete-time integral resonant control of negative imaginary systems,” Control Engineering Practice, 2025.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
The Intuition: Beyond Passivity
In control theory, we often use Passivity to guarantee stability. Passivity models systems where energy is dissipated, typically relating Force \(\to\) Velocity.
But many physical systems (like piezoelectric actuators, optical mirrors, and MEMS) are defined by the relationship between Force \(\to\) Position.
Negative Imaginary (NI) theory fills this gap. It captures the “spring-like” behavior of flexible structures where position lags force by between 0 and 180 degrees.


🏃 Passivity
Relating Force to Velocity

Phase Lag: \([-90^\circ, +90^\circ]\)
Physics: Dampers, Resistors.
Key Limit: Requires velocity measurements (often noisy).



📍 Negative Imaginary
Relating Force to Position

Phase Lag: \([0^\circ, -180^\circ]\)
Physics: Springs, Masses, Piezo-actuators.
Key Advantage: Works directly with high-precision position sensors.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
The “Holy Grail” of Robustness
The reason NI theory is so powerful for continuous-time systems is the DC Gain Stability Condition.
If you connect an NI Plant \(G(s)\) and an NI Controller \(C(s)\) in positive feedback, you don’t need to worry about high-frequency resonance modes (spillover). You only need to check the static (DC) gain:






\[\lambda_{max}(G(0)C(0)) < 1\]



This simple algebraic check guarantees stability for infinite-dimensional systems, making it incredibly robust against unmodeled dynamics.
[Image of feedback control loop diagram]

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
My Contributions to the Theory
While the linear theory is well-established, real-world systems are often nonlinear or require transformation to fit the NI framework. My research expands the boundaries of Continuous-Time NI Theory in three key directions.


1. Feedback Equivalence
Making systems NI
Not all systems are naturally NI. I derived necessary and sufficient conditions to determine if a generic linear system can be transformed into an NI system via state feedback. This expands the applicability of NI controllers to a much wider class of plants.

Paper: IEEE TAC, 2024



2. Nonlinear NI Systems
Beyond linear approximations
Real actuators saturate and exhibit nonlinear stiffness. I extended the theory to Nonlinear NI systems, proving that the stability properties hold even when the system dynamics are nonlinear, provided the potential energy is shaped correctly.

Paper: Automatica, 2023



3. Networked Consensus
Connecting multiple systems
I investigated the consensus problem for networks of heterogeneous nonlinear NI systems. This is critical for applications like formation flying or coupled micro-grids, where multiple NI agents must synchronize despite having different internal dynamics.

Paper: IEEE TAC, 2023

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
What is the NI viewpoint?
A useful way to understand negative imaginary (NI) systems is through the question:
If I apply a force, how does the position respond—and how does that interaction affect stability when I connect systems together?
Many physical systems (flexible structures, compliant actuators, nanopositioners) are naturally described by an input–output pair of the form

input: force / actuation (or voltage mapped to force)
output: displacement / position

For such systems, the most relevant “interaction variable” is often position, not velocity. NI theory formalizes a structural property of this force → position map that leads to simple and robust stability results for feedback interconnections.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
A physics anchor: mass–spring–damper
Consider the standard mass–spring–damper model [ mx + dx + kx = u, ] where (u) is an applied force and (x) is position. The transfer function from (u) to (x) is [ G(s) = = . ]
Two observations are worth keeping in mind:

The map (u x) (force → velocity) is naturally associated with power (ux), and this is the setting where passivity is most directly expressed.
The map (u x) (force → position) captures the elastic/inertial interaction directly. In many precision systems, (x) is measured with much higher fidelity than (x), and the stability-limiting dynamics are often tied to how position responds under force through flexible modes.

NI theory is designed for the second viewpoint.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
section: NI vs passivity: same spirit, different variables
text:
NI vs passivity: same spirit, different variables
Passivity is an energy-balance concept most naturally tied to effort → flow pairs (e.g., force → velocity, voltage → current). It is powerful, but it is not always the most natural description when the measured or controlled output is position.
NI systems can be viewed as a complementary framework tailored to force → position interactions that arise from spring–mass physics and flexible dynamics.
A practical way to remember the distinction is:

passivity is “well-behaved” in the power variable (u^y),
NI is “well-behaved” in an integrated variable, where (y) behaves like a generalized position.

This is why NI methods are often natural for flexible structures and nanopositioning: they match the sensors (position) and the dominant physics (compliance/inertia).

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
A compact frequency-domain signature
For linear time-invariant systems, NI is commonly characterized in the frequency domain.
For a (square) transfer matrix (G(s)), the NI property imposes a sign condition on [ j(G(j)-G(j)^*), >0, ] together with mild regularity conditions (e.g., no poles in the open right-half plane, and appropriate behavior at poles on the imaginary axis in the “standard” definition).
You do not need this expression to use the intuition, but it is the mathematical object that encodes the idea that the force → position map has a structured phase behavior consistent with compliant physical dynamics.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
section: The core payoff: stability of interconnections
text:
The core payoff: stability of interconnections
NI theory is most valuable when you connect systems.
Suppose (G(s)) is an NI plant and (C(s)) is an NI controller, and they are interconnected in positive feedback. Under standard NI assumptions, closed-loop stability can often be verified using a low-frequency (DC) condition of the form [ _{}!(G(0)C(0)) < 1. ]
The key message is not the exact inequality—it is the type of result:

stability can be concluded from a simple static gain check, without requiring accurate modeling of high-frequency flexible modes.

This is precisely the regime where spillover and unmodeled resonances make classical “model-accurate” design fragile. NI theory replaces detailed high-frequency modeling with a structural stability mechanism.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
section: Where NI systems appear in practice
text:
Where NI systems appear in practice
NI structure arises (or can be induced) in many systems where actuation interacts with compliance and inertia, including:

flexible mechanical structures and lightly damped resonant systems,
precision positioning devices (e.g., piezo-actuated nanopositioners),
electromechanical systems where the dominant measured variable is displacement,
networked physical systems where interaction is mediated through “spring-like” couplings.

This breadth is a major reason NI theory is useful: it captures a recurring physical pattern rather than a single application.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
section: What I work on in NI theory
text:
What I work on in NI theory
My research develops NI theory and NI-based control design in directions motivated by modern implementation constraints:

Discrete-time / digital NI theory
Extending NI concepts to sampled-data and discrete-time settings so that stability mechanisms remain valid when controllers are implemented digitally.
Nonlinear NI perspectives
Developing NI-like stability mechanisms for nonlinear systems, where physical structure (e.g., potential energy) can be used to preserve the interaction properties behind NI stability.
NI ideas in modern control workflows
Connecting NI structure with learning-enabled control design, with the aim of preserving stability-oriented structure while leveraging data-driven components.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
1. The Intuition: “Pushing a Spring”
What is the most intuitive way to think about a Negative Imaginary (NI) system?
Think of a simple mechanical spring with a position sensor. When you apply a force (input) to a spring, it stretches to a certain position (output).

The displacement is in phase with the force at low frequencies (DC).
As you vibrate it faster (near resonance), the position starts to lag.
Crucially, the position lag never exceeds 180 degrees.

This specific phase behavior—where the output “sloshes” behind the input but doesn’t completely flip sign—is the essence of Negative Imaginary systems.


🔬 Nanopositioners
In Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM), the piezoelectric stage is an NI system. We apply voltage (Force) and measure displacement (Position).


🦾 Flexible Robotics
A lightweight robotic arm is flexible. The relationship between torque applied at the joint and the angle of the tip is often Negative Imaginary.


⚡ Power Grids
In modern power systems, the “Swing Equation” relating power injection to rotor angle exhibits NI properties, which is key for frequency control.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
2. NI vs. Passivity: The Distinction
Engineers are often familiar with Passivity, but NI is distinct. The difference lies in what we measure.








Feature
Passivity
Negative Imaginary




Input \(\to\) Output
Force \(\to\) Velocity
Force \(\to\) Position


Physics
Dampers, Resistors (Dissipative)
Springs, Capacitors (Energy Storing)


Phase Lag
\([-90^\circ, +90^\circ]\)
\([0^\circ, -180^\circ]\)


Sensors
Velocity sensors (often noisy)
Position sensors (clean, precise)

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
3. Formal Definition
Mathematically, we define an NI system by looking at its frequency response.






NoteDefinition: Negative Imaginary System



A square, real, rational, proper transfer function matrix \(G(s)\) is Negative Imaginary if:

\(G(s)\) has no poles in the open Right Half Plane (RHP).
For all \(\omega > 0\) such that \(j\omega\) is not a pole of \(G(s)\), the following condition holds: \[
j(G(j\omega) - G^*(j\omega)) \geq 0
\]



In simpler terms, this ensures the Nyquist plot of \(G(j\omega)\) stays strictly in the “lower half” of the complex plane for positive frequencies.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
4. The Stability Result (The “Holy Grail”)
The reason NI theory is so powerful is the Simple Stability Condition.
When you connect an NI Plant \(G(s)\) with a strictly NI Controller \(C(s)\) in a positive feedback loop, the internal stability of the closed-loop system is guaranteed if and only if the DC Gain Condition is satisfied:






Tip



\[\lambda_{max}(G(0)C(0)) < 1\]


Why this matters: This condition depends only on the static (DC) gain. It is independent of high-frequency dynamics. This means your system is robust against unmodeled high-frequency resonances (spillover), a major advantage over standard robust control methods like \(H_\infty\).

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
5. History & My Contributions
Negative Imaginary theory is a relatively modern development in control theory. My work focuses on expanding this theory from linear, continuous cases to complex, nonlinear, and networked scenarios.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
2. Physical Interpretations
While the definition is mathematical, the NI property naturally captures the dynamics of specific physical relationships.

The Canonical Example: Mass-Spring System
The most fundamental example of an NI system is a mechanical mass-spring-damper system where: * Input: Force applied to the mass. * Output: Position (displacement) of the mass.
[Image of mass spring damper system diagram]
Unlike passive systems (which relate force to velocity), the force-to-position map inherently exhibits the phase lag characteristic of NI systems.


Engineering Applications
NI theory has proven highly effective in modeling and controlling a wide range of engineering systems beyond simple mechanics.



🔬 Nanopositioning
In Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM), the piezoelectric tube scanner is modeled as an NI system (voltage input \(\to\) displacement output).


⚡ Power Systems
The swing equation in power grids, which relates power injection to rotor angle, exhibits NI behavior. This is critical for modern frequency control.


🔌 Electrical Circuits
Certain electrical circuits, particularly those composed of specific arrangements of capacitors and inductors (energy storage elements), satisfy the NI property.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
3. The Core Value: Robust Stability
The primary motivation for using NI theory is the Simple Stability Condition.
When an NI Plant \(G(s)\) is interconnected with an NI Controller \(C(s)\) in a positive feedback loop, the closed-loop system is internally stable if and only if the DC Gain Condition is satisfied:






Tip



\[\lambda_{max}(G(0)C(0)) < 1\]


[Image of feedback control loop block diagram]
Why is this powerful? This condition depends only on the static (DC) gain. It is independent of the system’s high-frequency dynamics. This guarantees robust stability against unmodeled high-frequency spillover (e.g., infinite resonance modes in a flexible beam), provided those modes remain NI.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
4. Comparison with Passivity
Now that we understand NI systems, how do they relate to the more famous “Passivity” theory?
Both are energy-based stability tools, but they apply to different physical setups. Passivity is about Dissipation (Force \(\to\) Velocity), while NI is about Positioning (Force \(\to\) Position).

5. Evolution of the Theory
Negative Imaginary theory has evolved rapidly from a linear tool for flexible structures to a general framework for nonlinear and networked systems.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
2. The Canonical Example: Mechanical Systems
The most intuitive physical realization of an NI system is a mechanical structure with collocated force actuators and position sensors.
Consider a mass connected to a nonlinear spring: * Input (\(u\)): Force applied to the mass. * Output (\(y\)): Position (displacement) of the mass.



Mass-spring system illustration


Regardless of whether the spring is linear (\(F=kx\)) or nonlinear (\(F=kx^3\)), the system naturally satisfies the condition \(\dot{V} \leq u \dot{y}\). This makes NI theory a “natural language” for: * Micro-Robotics (Piezo-actuated stages) * Flexible Structures (Optical mirrors, crane arms) * Power Systems (Swing dynamics of generators)

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
section: 3. The Power of NI: Robust Stability
text:
3. The Power of NI: Robust Stability
The primary reason we study NI theory is for Robust Control.
In real engineering, models are never perfect. A flexible beam might have 100 vibration modes, but we might only model the first 3. Standard control methods often fail (go unstable) when those unmodeled high-frequency modes (“spillover”) get excited.
NI theory offers a powerful guarantee. If you connect an NI Plant \(G\) with an NI Controller \(C\) in a positive feedback loop, the system is stable if and only if:






Tip



DC Gain Condition: \(\quad \lambda_{max}(G(0)C(0)) < 1\)


[Image of feedback control loop block diagram]
The Key Insight: We only need to check the stability at “Zero Frequency” (DC). If it works at DC, the theory guarantees it works for all frequencies, even the unmodeled ones.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
2. Real-World Examples
The NI property naturally arises in a wide variety of physical systems.

Mechanical Systems with Collocated Sensors
A typical example of an NI system is a mechanical structure with collocated force actuators and position sensors.
Consider a generic flexible mechanical body (e.g., a beam, a bridge, or a robotic link) with the following input and output ports:

Input (\(u\)): Force (or Torque) applied at a specific point.
Output (\(y\)): Displacement (or Angle) measured at the same point.

In such a configuration, the energy dissipation inequality shown above is guaranteed by the conservation of energy. Hence, regardless of the complexity of the structure, the relationship between the applied force and the resulting displacement inherently satisfies the NI property.
Below are some example NI systems in engineering applications:



🔬 Nanopositioning
In Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM), piezoelectric actuators are used to scan samples. The dynamics from applied voltage (Force) to scanner displacement (Position) are NI.


🦾 Robotic Arms
Lightweight or soft robotic manipulators often exhibit significant flexibility. The dynamic relationship between the torque applied at a joint and the resulting joint angle captures these flexible modes and satisfies the NI property.


⚡ Power Systems
Modern power grids can be modeled as NI systems. Specifically, the “Swing Equation” which relates power injection to rotor angle is an NI dynamic, essential for frequency stability.

title: Negative Imaginary Systems Theory
text:
3. Stability & Contributions
The core utility of NI theory is robust stability. A fundamental result is that an NI system can be stabilized using another strictly NI system in a positive feedback configuration.
One of my research contribution is in providing a nonlinear NI systems theory. See the following articles:

MTNS2020
IEEE TAC 2023


Key Research Articles

Necessary and sufficient conditions for state feedback equivalence to negative imaginary systems IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, 2024 I derived the mathematical conditions to determine when a general system can be transformed into an NI system via state feedback, significantly expanding the applicability of NI control methods.


Making nonlinear systems negative imaginary via state feedback Automatica, 2023 This work extends the theory to the nonlinear domain. We proved that by reshaping the potential energy (via feedback), a nonlinear system can be rendered NI, ensuring stability even with nonlinear stiffness.


Output feedback consensus for networked heterogeneous nonlinear negative-imaginary systems IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, 2023 I established stability results for networks of multiple heterogeneous NI agents. This provides a theoretical foundation for synchronizing robotic swarms or coupled microgrids.

The core utility of NI theory is robust stability. A fundamental result is that an NI system can be stabilized using another strictly NI system in a positive feedback configuration.
